stages.name: No evidence
stages.desc: No dated Phoenician find in our sources, or too little excavated

stages.name: Local only
stages.desc: Known local communities, no clear Phoenician link

stages.name: Trading contact
stages.desc: Local sites with Phoenician goods or ideas

stages.name: Phoenician settlement
stages.desc: At least one site proposed as a Phoenician foundation or community

stages.name: Successor towns
stages.desc: Local towns of Phoenician tradition, in Gadir's trading world

states.name: Évora
timeline: Late Bronze Age hillforts of the Serra d'Ossa, soon to be abandoned
Small farms and cemeteries with imported glass, as at Tera, near Mora
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Portalegre
timeline: Little securely dated evidence for this period
The hillfort of Cabeço de Vaiamonte belongs to the local Iron Age
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Viana do Castelo
timeline: The walled castro of Coto da Pena watches the mouth of the Minho
Coto da Pena and Santo Estêvão da Facha are listed among sites with sparse southern influence
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Castelo Branco
timeline: Hillforts of the Beira, where early iron had already arrived along inland routes
Cachouça, near Idanha-a-Nova, keeps contact with the Mediterranean world
Occupation at Cachouça ends after the sixth century BC
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Guarda
timeline: Hillforts such as São Romão, near Seia, in an older Bronze Age exchange network
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Bragança
timeline: Hill settlements are known, but no Phoenician find of this age in the sources used here
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Vila Real
timeline: Local communities of the upper Tâmega and Douro valleys
Imports are noted at Cidadelhe, but dated only loosely, between the fifth and second centuries BC
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Braga
timeline: Hilltop castros such as São Julião and Barbudo; no Phoenician settlement known
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Faro
timeline: Late Bronze Age communities live at Tavira and Castro Marim, above the estuaries
Tavira: a wall with inner compartments and ritual pits, read as a Phoenician community on an older local site
Cerro da Rocha Branca, on the Arade near Silves: rectangular buildings inside a straight-sided wall
Castro Marim, usually read as a local town, takes up Phoenician building and pottery
Tavira's Phoenician phase has ended; Castro Marim carries on, supplied from the Gadir region
Attic Greek cups and western amphorae reach Castro Marim
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Beja
timeline: Castro dos Ratinhos: an eastern-style shrine inside a local hilltop settlement
Ratinhos is abandoned; hilltop powers of the interior collapse
Rural cemeteries with glass beads, amber and scarabs; gravestones in a script adapted from Phoenician signs
Fernão Vaz is abandoned and inscribed gravestones fade; some Mediterranean imports still reach the Guadiana
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Setúbal
timeline: Small Late Bronze Age farmsteads such as Quinta do Marcelo, with a few early iron knives
Quinta do Almaraz: a settlement with a defensive ditch on the Tagus, perhaps paired with Lisbon
Abul: a square building of foreign type rises on empty ground beside the Sado
Alcácer do Sal's cemetery receives scarabs, Phoenician-type jars and an ostrich-egg vessel
Abul is abandoned; Alcácer do Sal and Setúbal remain as local towns
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Lisbon
timeline: Small farming sites such as Praça da Figueira, below the castle hill
First right-angled buildings at the foot of the castle hill, with Phoenician pottery
Phoenician letters scratched on a jar on the castle hill
The settlement spreads over the hill; a gravestone is cut in Phoenician in this century
Lisbon's potters go their own way: a regional style grown from Phoenician models
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Santarém
timeline: A Late Bronze Age community on the Alcáçova plateau above the Tagus
Jars from the Málaga coast and red-slip plates reach Santarém, where most pots are still handmade
Santarém remains the chief town of the middle Tagus
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Leiria
timeline: No dated Phoenician site in the sources used here; ships passed on the way to the Mondego
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Coimbra
timeline: A Late Bronze Age community at Conímbriga
Santa Olaia, at the mouth of the Mondego: probably a Phoenician foundation, with metalworking
Conímbriga, upstream, takes up wheel-made pottery from the coast
Santa Olaia lingers or empties (scholars differ: about 500 or after 400 BC); Conímbriga endures
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Aveiro
timeline: Small fortified villages (castros) between the Vouga and the Douro
Punic amphorae reach the castro of Romariz
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Porto
timeline: Open and fortified villages at Baião and along the Douro
Punic commerce touches coastal castros such as Porto's Morro da Sé and Terroso
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

states.name: Viseu
timeline: The bronze hoard of Baiões shows Mediterranean links older than any Phoenician port in Portugal
After the Bronze Age hoards, little new Mediterranean material is known here
states.untouched: No dated Phoenician evidence in the sources used here.

events.title: Gadir trades west
events.text: The Phoenician colony of Gadir, today's Cádiz, is the gateway from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.

events.title: Huelva's silver
events.text: At Huelva, eastern merchants had been trading for silver since at least the ninth century BC.

events.title: Shrine at Ratinhos
events.text: A rectangular, three-roomed shrine of eastern plan stands among the round huts of a local hilltop settlement.

events.title: Baiões hoard
events.text: Bronzes from the hilltop of Baiões mix Atlantic, inland and Mediterranean styles, before any Phoenician port is known in Portugal.

events.title: Iron at Marcelo
events.text: Iron knives from Quinta do Marcelo, opposite Lisbon, belong to the last Bronze Age farms or to the first contacts.

events.title: Farms below Lisbon
events.text: Before any town on the castle hill, people farmed at small sites such as Praça da Figueira.

events.title: Castros of the Minho
events.text: Walled villages such as Coto da Pena watch the northern river mouths.

events.title: Málaga jars, Santarém
events.text: Amphorae imported from the Málaga coast lie in the lowest Iron Age levels of Santarém's Alcáçova.

events.title: Tavira's wall
events.text: A massive wall with inner compartments is raised at Tavira in the eighth century BC; it later reaches 9.5 metres in thickness.

events.title: First buildings, Lisbon
events.text: Right-angled walls and harbour works at the former Sommer warehouses are among Lisbon's oldest, from the late eighth century BC.

events.title: Almaraz fortified
events.text: Quinta do Almaraz, facing Lisbon across the Tagus, is settled and defended by a broad ditch.

events.title: Ratinhos abandoned
events.text: The shrine and settlement of Ratinhos fall out of use as the hilltop powers of the interior decline.

events.title: Handmade pots, Lisbon
events.text: In one of Lisbon's oldest layers, at Rua de São Mamede, 61 per cent of the pottery is local and handmade.

events.title: Pits of Tavira
events.text: Rock-cut pits receive red-slip plates, incense burners and a pendant linked to Astarte; some see the cult of Baal.

events.title: Rocha Branca
events.text: A walled cluster of rectangular buildings stands on the Arade near Silves; its earliest date is debated.

events.title: Potters of the Tagus
events.text: Wheel-made jars and red-slip plates are now made on the Tagus itself, in western Phoenician fashion.

events.title: Santa Sofia
events.text: At Santa Sofia, near Vila Franca de Xira, a strongly local village uses amphorae and red-slip ware.

events.title: Letters on a jar
events.text: Phoenician letters, perhaps a place name, are scratched on an amphora on Lisbon's castle hill.

events.title: Castro Marim changes
events.text: Above the mouth of the Guadiana, an old local settlement takes up Phoenician building and pottery.

events.title: Santa Olaia
events.text: A walled settlement with a mole and metal workshops rises at the mouth of the Mondego, with no older village beneath.

events.title: Abul
events.text: On the Sado, a square building with a courtyard is founded on empty ground: trading post, sanctuary, or both.

events.title: A Phoenician gravestone
events.text: In the seventh century BC a Lisbon gravestone is cut in Phoenician, with names that look local.

events.title: Tavira's cremations
events.text: Four burials of the seventh century BC at the Graça convent hold ashes in pits and painted urns.

events.title: Kolaios in Tartessos
events.text: Herodotus says a storm drove the Greek captain Kolaios beyond the Pillars to Tartessos, where he made a fortune.

events.title: The Southwest script
events.text: Gravestones of the Alentejo and Algarve carry a local script, its signs adapted largely from Phoenician.

events.title: Conímbriga's new pots
events.text: Inland from Santa Olaia, the older community of Conímbriga takes up southern goods.

events.title: Cachouça
events.text: In the Beira interior, the hillfort of Cachouça is occupied into the sixth century BC with Mediterranean links.

events.title: Fonte Velha stones
events.text: Inscribed stones mark burials at Fonte Velha de Bensafrim, near Lagos.

events.title: Corinthian cups, Almaraz
events.text: Greek pottery made at Corinth between 600 and 575 BC reaches Almaraz, along with scarabs and alabaster.

events.title: Alcácer's cemetery
events.text: At Alcácer do Sal, graves hold Egyptian-type scarabs, a bronze jug and an ostrich-egg vessel.

events.title: Tyre submits
events.text: After a long Babylonian siege, the mother city of Gadir comes under Babylon's power.

events.title: Vinha das Caliças
events.text: Near Beja, farming communities bury their dead with glass beads, amber and scarabs.

events.title: Glass at Tera
events.text: Rural cemeteries such as Tera, near Mora, carry imported glass into central Alentejo.

events.title: Ships on clay
events.text: Tagus potters and scribblers leave model boats and drawings of ships at Lisbon and Almaraz.

events.title: Santa Olaia grows
events.text: Metalworking quarters thicken at Santa Olaia during the sixth century BC.

events.title: Tavira's Phoenicians fade
events.text: Tavira's Phoenician phase ends during or after the sixth century BC.

events.title: Abul abandoned
events.text: Abul is deserted by about the end of the sixth century BC, while Alcácer do Sal lives on.

events.title: Himilco's voyage
events.text: Roman writers say the Carthaginian Himilco explored the Atlantic coasts of Europe; the date is uncertain.

events.title: Punic jars at Romariz
events.text: Punic amphorae of the fifth century BC travel north to a castro near the Douro.

events.title: Fernão Vaz ends
events.text: The building at Fernão Vaz, near Ourique, is abandoned around the middle of the fifth century BC.

events.title: Traders at Porto
events.text: The castro on Porto's cathedral hill is among those drawn into Punic commerce from the fifth century BC.

events.title: Attic cups, Castro Marim
events.text: Greek cups from Athens arrive at Castro Marim with goods from the Gadir region.

events.title: Inscribed graves cease
events.text: By the end of the fifth century BC the carved tombs and inscribed stones of the southwest have disappeared.

chartNote: Share of mainland Portugal's area, by today's 18 districts. Each district takes the colour of its best-known site, so one excavation can colour a whole district. This is a deliberate simplification: 'Phoenician settlement' means proposed by archaeologists, not proven, and many scholars read the same sites as local towns. Years are estimates within a generation or two, on the pottery chronology; radiocarbon often points earlier. 'No evidence' also reflects where little has been dug.
